peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Dear Editor,
We sincerely appreciate the time and effort that the Editor and Reviewers have
dedicated to providing valuable and constructive feedback on our manuscript,
NCOMMS-24-47215-T, titled "YTHDF3 predicts neoadjuvant chemotherapy
response and outcomes in Esophageal Squamous Cell Carcinoma". In response to the
reviewers' suggestions, we have carefully considered each comment and conducted
additional experiments and analyses to clarify and strengthen our findings.
We believe the revisions we have made substantially improve the quality, depth
and novelty of the manuscript and satisfy all of the reviewer's comments.
We respectfully request that the Editor consider the manuscript for publication in Nature
Communications. We greatly appreciate the opportunity to submit this revised
manuscript.
Below, we provide a point-by-point response to each of the reviewers’ comments
and outline our revisions.
Reviewers' comments:
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript, Wang X. et al reported a predictive role of YTHDF3 in
paclitaxel-based NACT by upregulating INCENP and CDCA8. It have been well-
reported that either YTHDF3 or METTL3 are associated with poor prognosis of many
cancers. Authors firstly reported the m6A-modification dependent role of YTHDF3 to
promote the translation of INCENP and CDCA8, which was not surprising at all.
1, The mechanism of INCENP and CDCA8 to confer paclitaxel non-response should be
the major novelty of this study, which was completely missing.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We have now focus on the role of
INCENP and CDCA8 in paclitaxel non-response and the mechanism of INCENP and
CDCA8 to confer NACT non-response have deeply researched. Accordingly, we have
revised the manuscript to reflect these key findings:
(1) INCENP and CDCA8 is a critical component of the chromosome passenger
complex (CPC), however, the role of INCENP and CDCA8 in regulating NACT
resistance remains unexplored. Our analysis of tumor tissue from NACT patients
showed that INCENP and CDCA8 were significantly upregulated in non-responders
across various cancer types (Fig. 1 and Fig. 7, line361). And we validated that knocking
down INCENP and CDCA8 enhanced the sensitivity of paclitaxel and cisplatin (Fig.
2).
(2) We have clarified that the mechanism of INCENP and CDCA8 to confer paclitaxel
non-response in revised manuscript (Fig. 3-6). In detail, inhibition of INCENP and
CDCA8 promotes multipolar spindle formation, resulting in more severe mitotic
defects, leading to enhanced paclitaxel efficacy and increased cell death, thus
improving NACT response to patient. In non-responders, the upregulation of INCENP
and CDCA8 results from m6A modification recognized by YTHDF3, leading to
enhanced translation, ultimately leading to NACT resistance. Following Mechanism
diagram explained it in detail:
2, In 4e/f, knock-down of INCENP and CDCA8 inhibited cell growth in the absence of
paclitaxel, indicating that the upregulation of INCENP and CDCA8 may render poor
prognosis irrespective of paclitaxel treatment.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We agree with your comments that
INCENP and CDCA8, as key regulators of mitosis, play an important role in cell
proliferation. Our study is focus on searching biomarkers to predict patient response to
NACT and improve 5-year survival rate, avoiding patients suffer from the toxic side
effects of chemotherapy. And we identified that reliable biomarkers INCENP and
CDCA8 predict patient responsiveness to NACT across various cancer types.
3, In 4K, knock-down of YTHDF3 inhibited cell growth significantly in the absence of
paclitaxel and the growth-inhibition of YTHDF3 KD cells seems to be significantly
more sensitive to paclitaxel with the difference quite moderate.
Response: Thank you for your constructive suggestions, as well as those from
Reviewer #4. Upon careful consideration, we recognized that the limitations in our
initial experimental design may have contributed to the moderate results observed. To
address this, we have optimized our experimental methodology and using a wider range
of paclitaxel and cisplatin concentrations to assess the effect of YTHDF3 KD on
paclitaxel and cisplatin sensitivity. These improvements obtain more robust and
statistically significant results, as demonstrated in the revised manuscript (Fig. 3c, d).
4, Authors should make clear that it is paclitaxel-based NACT but not NACT in general
and point out INCENP and CDCA8 in the title.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive feedback. we have made it
clear that the regimes of NACT are paclitaxel plus cisplatin in revised manuscript. And
the novel title of this article is "INCENP and CDCA8 predict neoadjuvant
chemotherapy response and outcomes in pan-cancer".
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Wang et al. are evaluating the role of YTHDF3 in neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT)
for esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). The authors identify YTHDF3 as a
critical mediator of poor response to paclitaxel-based NACT, link YTHDF3's regulation
of INCENP and CDCA8 mRNA translation in an m6A-dependent manner to enhanced
cell division, thus offering a mechanistic explanation for its role in NACT resistance.
This study is exploring an important topic. The manuscript reads well, with a clear and
logical flow throughout. The data is compelling for the most part, and extensive
analysis has been performed to substantiate the role of YTHDF3 in NACT resistance in
esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC). To improve this manuscript, the authors
should address the following points.
Major comments:
1. The authors used a heatmap to claim that 9 m6A regulators were upregulated in non-
responders (Fig. 1b). However, I noticed that the sixth responder (from the left) also
exhibited a more pronounced upregulation of these 9 m6A regulators. Conversely, the
sixth and ninth non-responders showed decreased expression of m6A regulators,
including YTHDF3, which the authors highlighted. The authors should address these
observations in the manuscript to clarify the interpretation of this data. Additionally,
the selection of YTHDF3 as a candidate is not strongly justified based on the heatmap.
Furthermore, the authors mention METTL3 in later sections; therefore, its expression
should also be shown in this heatmap. The authors should also clarify what the "p"
denotes beside the heatmap in the figure legend.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments. In previous manuscript, Figure 1b
presented sequencing data from paclitaxel-based NACT samples. According to the
reviewer’s suggestion and to ensure consistency in treatment regimen, we have now
focused our analysis exclusively on patients who received the cisplatin plus paclitaxel
NACT regimen throughout our study. We have also performed additionally sequencing
to supply cohort1 (supplementary table 1). Subsequent analysis revealed that YTHDF3
exhibited the most significantly differentially expressed protein among the 20 m6A
regulatory proteins, and the expression level of METTL3 was analysis and has no
changes in non-responders. Additionally, we have clarified the statistical significance
("p") in the revised Figure 1c to improve transparency.
2. The authors used a heatmap and GSEA results to claim that INCENP and CDCA8
are regulated by YTHDF3 and subsequently identified these two genes as downstream
targets of YTHDF3. However, there are other candidates listed, and the authors should
clarify the criteria used to select these two genes.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comments. In the manuscript (line 114), we
clarified that GO enrichment and GESA analysis highlighted the chromosomal
passenger complex (CPC) in the cellular component section as the top altered pathway
and involved in mitotic nuclear division by proteomics analysis in shYTHDF3 ESCC
cells (Fig.1d, e). Importantly, GSEA analysis revealed that key proteins in the CPC,
including INCENP, CDCA8, and AURKB, were significantly downregulated in
shYTHDF3 cells. Western blotting confirmed that INCENP and CDCA8 showed more
pronounced changes in both shYTHDF3 and OE-YTHDF3 ESCC cell lines
(Supplementary Fig. 1e-h), therefore, we selected and continued to research INCENP
and CDCA8.
3. The authors used the same scale bar for Fig. 4a and Fig. 4c, implying that the figures
should display cells with the same size. However, it appears that the cells in Fig. 4c are
smaller than those in Fig. 4a, leading to some ambiguity in interpreting the results. The
authors should clarify whether this discrepancy is due to a typo error or some other
reasons.
Response: Thank you for your careful consideration. We sincerely apologize for our
mistakes, we have clarified Fig. 4c in the revised manuscript as show in Supplementary
Fig. 1i, and have indicated the scale bar in the figure legend.
4. The authors used Western blotting to show the expression levels of INCENP and
CDCA8 in Fig. 5a, Fig. 5m, Fig. 6c, and Fig. 7j. However, there are inconsistencies in
the bands presented. For example, INCENP shows two bands in KYSE30 cells in Fig.
6c, whereas other figures display only one band. Similarly, CDCA8 appears to have a
faint band above the main band in Fig. 5a and Fig. 6c, but other figures show only a
single, clear band. These inconsistencies need to be addressed to ensure data reliability.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful observation regarding the inconsistencies in
the Western blot bands for INCENP and CDCA8 across the figures. Upon reviewing
the data, the band inconsistencies are due to the use of different antibody clones.
Therefore, the same antibody was standardized for all WB experiments to ensure
consistency. The expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 in Fig. 5a and Fig. 6c
display clearer and more consistent bands across all figures (Fig. 4a, b and
Supplementary Fig. 1e, g).
5. The authors investigated the regulation of INCENP and CDCA8 by YTHDF3
throughout the manuscript. However, it remains unclear which of these factors is more
critical as a downstream effector of YTHDF3. Fig. 7i suggests that either INCENP or
CDCA8 can rescue the phenotype of multipolar spindle formation in shYTHDF3 cells.
The authors should discuss this in more detail to clarify the relative importance of these
factors.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment. Both INCENP
and CDCA8 are core components of the Chromosomal Passenger Complex (CPC) and
are functionally indispensable for proper mitotic progression. Our rescue experiments
demonstrated that overexpression of either INCENP or CDCA8 in YTHDF3 KD cells
effectively reversed the increased sensitivity to paclitaxel and cisplatin, highlighting
their functional importance downstream of YTHDF3. While INCENP showed a slightly
stronger rescue effect, both proteins are essential mediators of YTHDF3-driven
chemoresistance (Fig. 3o, p).
6. In Figures 5a and 6c, rescue effect of YTHDF3 on CDCA8 and INCENP expression
is ambiguous. Data needs to be normalized for GAPDH and multiple experiments
performed and plotted.
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback. we have now normalized the
expression levels of CDCA8 and INCENP to GAPDH. And we have updated the figures
to include the normalized data across multiple experiments (Supplementary Fig. 4b, c).
7. For figure 5b and 5c, the authors stated that YTHDF3 affected the protein levels of
INCENP and CDCA8. As YTHDF3 promotes cell proliferation, how can the authors
substantiate that the alterations in protein levels of INCENP and CDCA8 are
attributable to YTHDF3 expression rather than changes in cell number?
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. To address the concern about cell
number, we used ImageJ to quantify the relative protein expression levels of INCENP
and CDCA8, normalizing them to the total cell number. This ensures that the observed
changes in protein levels reflect the effect of YTHDF3 expression rather than
differences in cell number. We have also clarified how the IF images were collected and
quantified (line 594).
8. The observation that eIF3A and YTHDF3 can also be precipitated by IgG (Figure 5i)
should be repeated and interpreted.
Response: Thank you for your detailed and helpful suggestions. We found that protein
A/G magnetic beads were not thoroughly washed during the experimental procedure,
resulting in non-specific bands. To address this, we have repeated the experiment with
more stringent washing steps to ensure that no bead-associated proteins eIF3A and
YTHDF3 were co-precipitated with the IgG (Fig. 5j, k).
9. The data looks pretty good in figure 8e and 8f, may I know which one is more
important for the prediction the clinical outcomes of NACT response.
Response: Thank you for your insightful suggestions. Considering that INCENP and
CDCA8 are both essential subunits of the chromosomal passenger complex, the loss of
either INCENP or CDCA8 severely compromises CPC function. Therefore, INCENP
and CDCA8 are likely to be equally important in predicting clinical responses to NACT.
We have now discussed this point in the revised manuscript to clarify the importance
of both factors in predicting clinical outcomes (line448).
Minor comments:
1. Statistics are not always shown in figures. This needs to be addressed for each panel
(e.g., Western blots and IF, IHC staining).
Response: Thank you for your constructive feedback. We agree that the inclusion of
statistical analysis is important to enhance the clarity and robustness of the results. We
have presented the statistical data for the western blots in the Supplementary Fig. 2-6,
and have statistically validated and clearly interpreted IF and IHC panels. The figure
legends have also been updated accordingly to reflect these changes.
2. Most of the figures are densely populated. Font size is pretty small, making it hard to
decipher certain figures.
Response: Thank you for your valuable feedback. We have carefully revised the figures
to improve their clarity. The font size has been increased to ensure figures are easily
decipherable.
3. P6 line 216, should it be fig. 4e, f?
Response: Thank you for your detailed and helpful suggestions. We have carefully
reviewed the manuscript to prevent such errors.
4: P3 line 106, the brackets should include IHC instead of Immunohistochemistry
staining.
Response: Thank you for your careful reading. We have revised the brackets in the
revised manuscript (line 130).
P4 line 147, “proteomics sequencing” is not a proper terminology.
Response: Thank you for highlighting it. The term “proteomics sequencing” has been
revised to “proteomic analysis” in the revised manuscript (Line 115) to ensure
terminological accuracy.
P12 line 422, there is an incorrect back bracket.
Response: We appreciate your attention to detail. The incorrect back bracket on Page
12, Line 422 has been corrected in the revised manuscript (line 497).
P12 line 424, Should it be 70 μm strainer?
Response: Thank you for your detailed and helpful suggestions. The correct
specification is a "70 μm strainer" as stated in Line 499.
P12 line 443, it should be 0.45-μm PVDF membrane.
Response: Thank you for highlighting it. The correct specification is a "0.45 μm PVDF
membrane " as stated in Line 515.
P13 line 462, “Te cells” should be revised.
Response: Thank you for your careful reading. "Te cells" has been revised to "The
cells" in Line 534 of the revised manuscript.
P39 Supplementary Fig. 1b, “Ggrade II” should be revised.
Response: We appreciate your attention to detail. We have double-checked the
manuscript and figures to avoid these similar errors.
5. Other grammar and typo issues, eg., line 111 “. and”, line 194 “, (Fig. 3d)”.
Response: Thank you for your rigorous review. We have meticulously proofread the
manuscript to eliminate any spelling, grammatical, or typographical errors and to ensure
linguistic accuracy.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
YTHDF3 predicts neoadjuvant chemotherapy response and outcomes in Esophageal
Squamous Cell Carcinoma by Xiangyu Wang, have studied the role of YTH domain-
containing family protein 3 (YTHDF3) in predicting poor responses to neoadjuvant
chemotherapy (NACT) in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) patients.
YTHDF3 enhances cell mitosis by regulating the translation of specific mRNAs, leading
to diminished effectiveness of paclitaxel-based NACT. High levels of YTHDF3 correlate
with worse patient outcomes. The study suggests that Targeting YTHDF3 not only
improves responses to chemotherapy but also offers a potential therapeutic strategy to
enhance treatment efficacy and survival rates in cancer patients.
YTHDF3 is crucial for predicting outcomes in breast cancer and hepatocellular
carcinoma. Previous studies have established a YTHDF3-based model for overall
survival prediction. While research on esophageal cancer has been limited, the
mechanisms underlying YTHDF3 overexpression are now understood. The authors'
study of YTHDF3 upregulation in esophageal cancer, alongside the use of paclitaxel as
a neoadjuvant chemotherapy agent and its associated sensitivity, could provide a
significant contribution worthy of publication in Nature Communications.
--One of the major criticism for this manuscript is, multiple way of action of Paclitaxel
has been identified, till Paclitaxel is in the clinic. There are seminal publications by
Antonio Fojo group and Fernando Cabral group more than decades ago stating that
Paclitaxel can inhibit cell division as a antimitotic agent, but can also inhibit, cell
migration and angiogenesis. The authors fully focused on the effect of cell division after
YTHDF3 overexpression. Though there are recent publications on the impact of YTDF3
on cell migration and angiogenesis, the authors overlooked that for this publication.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We fully agree that paclitaxel affects
not only cell division but also processes like angiogenesis and cell migration. In this
manuscript, we focus on identify reliable biomarkers that can predict neoadjuvant
chemotherapy sensitivity, aiming to avoid the toxic side effects of chemotherapy for
patients. Through our comprehensive investigation, we identified YTHDF3, INCENP
and CDCA8, can serve as reliable and effective biomarkers for predicting neoadjuvant
chemotherapy sensitivity, with particularly strong relevance across multiple cancer
types. Additionally, we observed that YTHDF3 KD altered the expression of cell
adhesion molecules (Supplementary Fig. 1c), which are involved in angiogenesis and
migration pathways, however, it ranked relatively low in significance in KEGG
pathway analysis, whereas cell cycle-related pathways, particularly those involving
mitotic regulation, were consistently ranked among the top five. Given this clear
enrichment and the strong correlation with the observed multipolar spindle formation
in YTHDF3 KD cells, we prioritized the mechanistic dissection of the cell division
pathway in this study. Therefore, we believe that YTHDF3, along with INCENP and
CDCA8, represents a more promising set of predictors for chemotherapy sensitivity.
--There are several items that can be improved before considered for publication. To
investigate the role of YTHDF3 in response to paclitaxel, the authors have assessed
whether inhibiting YTHDF3 could increase the sensitivity of ESCC cells to paclitaxel
treatment. The term “Adjacent” in Fig 1E or throughout the manuscript is difficult to
follow. What the authors meant by adjacent? Also , what is the basis for the selection
of “responders vs non responders.” The authors stated in the Fig 1n that elevated
YTHDF3 levels were negatively correlated with tumor remission rates (Fig. 1n). Did
the author found correlation coefficient? A graph showing reverse correlation will be
beneficial. Also which method the authors used to calculate correlation? There are
similar problems when the authors talk about positive and negative correlations, the
numbers and significance of the correlation should be provided.
Response: Thank you for your detailed and helpful suggestions.
--In Fig 1E, we have revised “Adjacent” revised into “Adjacent normal tissue” in
Supplementary Fig. 1i, j.
--And patients with evaluable responses were classified as responders (TRG0, 1) and
non-responders (TRG2, 3) based on the National Comprehensive Cancer Network
(NCCN) TRG criteria. [Ajani, J. A. et al. Esophageal and Esophagogastric Junction
Cancers, Version 2.2023, NCCN Clinical Practice Guidelines in Oncology. J Natl
Compr Canc Netw 21, 393-422, doi:10.6004/jnccn.2023.0019 (2023).]. We have
clarified it in the revised manuscript (line 92).
--We sincerely apologize for the confusion caused by the inaccurate description. The
tumor remission rate is not a continuous variable, so correlation coefficient analysis
cannot be applied to this metric.
--In the revised manuscript, we have included the correlation coefficients using Pearson
analysis to examine both positive and negative correlations, along with their
corresponding significance values. These changes are reflected in the updated figures
and figure legends (Fig.1h, 2a and b, 4p, 7f and g, Supplementary Fig. 3m, r and 7e).
--The authors have used YTDHF3 mutant. Are they dominant negative? If they are not
what is the rationale of using them, when the authors have already used shRNA and
mock sh RNA for their study. The authors have calculated mitotic sister chromatid
separation and nuclear envelop breakdown. Why the authors used both the methods?
Is it to rule out mitotic slippage? Better explanation is needed.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment.
-- The YTHDF3 mutant acts as a dominant negative regulator of INCENP and CDCA8
expression, thereby impairing cell division. YTHDF3 contains two hydrophobic
residues, W438 and W492, which are essential for specific recognition of m6A, and the
mutant form of YTHDF3 lacks this m6A-binding capability. While we have previously
used YTHDF3 shRNA to study its effect on cell division and the regulation of INCENP
and CDCA8, in order to investigate whether YTHDF3 regulates INCENP and CDCA8
in an m6A-dependent manner, we constructed a YTHDF3 mutant, and further
overexpressed the mutated YTHDF3 in YTHDF3 KD cells. This demonstrated that the
mutant YTHDF3 lost its regulatory effect on INCENP and CDCA8, thereby disrupting
cell division in an m6A-dependent manner.
--During mitosis, sister chromatid separation, nuclear envelope breakdown, and mitotic
slippage are key events. However, our proteomics analysis of shYTHDF3 cells enriched
only the pathways related to sister chromatid separation and nuclear envelope
breakdown. Therefore, we focused on these two pathways for our study, our intention
was not to exclude or rule out mitotic slippage. In our study, differential gene
enrichment analysis identified INCENP and CDCA8 as core components of the
chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), which is essential for proper chromosome
alignment, segregation, and cytokinesis. Downregulation of either INCENP or CDCA8
leads to defects in these processes, resulting in the formation of multipolar spindles,
disrupting mitotic progression, and potentially contributing to poor chemotherapy
response.
--The authors did not address the significance of the pathways impacted by YTDF3
downregulation, beyond those related to cell division. Given the availability of RNA
sequencing data, it would be valuable to explore additional effects on other signaling
pathways, such as those involved in cell migration or epithelial-to-mesenchymal
transition (EMT) and mesenchymal-to-epithelial transition (MET). A more thorough
examination of these pathways could enhance the novelty of the manuscript. A
significant limitation of the paper is the authors' focus solely on INCENP and CDCA8.
While the data clearly demonstrate effects on the cell division pathway, it's important
to note that the average cell division time in humans is around 90 days, with only about
2% of cells being mitotic at any given time. Additionally, Paclitaxel is administered at
maximum tolerable doses, leading to only a limited number of mitotic blocks in vivo
within the treatment window. This context may explain why the IHC data from patients
do not show an increased propensity for mitotic blockage. I encourage the authors to
discuss how YTHDF3 downregulation may affect or sensitize other antitumorigenic
pathways.
Response: We appreciate your suggestion to explore other signaling pathways. In our
proteomics analysis following YTHDF3 knockdown, we observed changes in the
expression of cell adhesion molecules, suggesting that YTHDF3 may also influence
cell migration or EMT/MET pathways. However, KEGG pathway enrichment analysis
ranked these pathways relatively low in significance, whereas cell cycle-related
pathways, particularly those involving mitotic regulation, were consistently ranked
among the top five (Supplementary Fig. 1c). Given this clear enrichment and the strong
correlation with the observed multipolar spindle formation in YTHDF3 KD cells, we
prioritized the mechanistic dissection of the cell division pathway in this study. We
acknowledge your point that only about 2% of cells are in mitosis at any given time in
humans, which may limit the overall impact of mitotic blockage by YTHDF3, INCENP
and CDCA8. However, our findings show that these proteins are significantly
upregulated in non-responder patients, making them particularly effective as predictive
biomarkers for NACT sensitivity. Our primary purpose is to identify reliable
biomarkers to help avoiding the unnecessary toxic effects of NACT.
We have now included a discussion on the potential roles of YTHDF3 in regulating
additional antitumorigenic pathways, such as EMT and cell migration. We fully agree
that a more thorough examination of these pathways could enhance the novelty and
breadth of the manuscript (line 422).
Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
The work described in the manuscript seeks to identify biomarkers predictive of clinical
response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) in patients with esophageal squamous
cell carcinoma (ESCC) before surgery. Using transcriptomic analyses in tumors from
patients who responded to paclitaxel-based NACT vs the non-responders, they
identified an enrichment for YTHDF3 transcript in the non-responders. YTHDF3 is a
cytoplasmic regulator of m6A (N6-methyladenosine). YTHDF3 was also upregulated in
cancer versus adjacent normal tissue, and correlated with higher clinical tumor stage
and tumor infiltration depth. They used many cell biology and multi-omics tools to
elaborate on a potential mechanism by which YTHDF3 induces the resistance
phenotype. Authors show that high levels of YTHDF3 upregulate the translation of
INCENP and CDCA8 transcripts (components of the chromosomal passenger complex)
by recruiting eID3A proteins to its target mRNAs. Authors speculate that using Ebselen,
a chemical inhibitor of YTHDF3, will induce defects in the mitotic spindle and sensitize
ESCC patients' response expressing high levels of YTHDF3 to paclitaxel. However,
there are major concerns for this manuscript as outlined below.
Major concerns:
1. Taxanes are mostly used in combination with cisplatin or carboplatin in the
neoadjuvant setting for ESCC. So, the correlations in the current study between the
YTHDF3 transcript and response to NACT treatment, refer to clinical response to the
drug cocktail used and not to paclitaxel specifically. Thus, the current study by
addressing mechanisms relevant to taxanes only, do not really address the clinical
problem of NACT failure in patients with ESCC.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comment. We fully agree
with taxanes are commonly used in combination with cisplatin or carboplatin in the
neoadjuvant setting for ESCC. To address this concern, we have systematically revised
our study design to specifically focus on the paclitaxel (taxanes) plus cisplatin
combination regimen throughout our investigation. This refinement ensures that our
findings directly address the mechanisms underlying NACT response and the critical
clinical challenge of treatment failure in ESCC patients receiving this standard
therapeutic regimen.
a. Thus, in Figure 1 clinical response does not reflect paclitaxel-only response and also
if the transcript is associated with response to treatment, overall survival is not the
appropriate metric. Instead they should use pathologic response prior to surgery.
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. In the previous manuscript, Figure
1 did not reflect the paclitaxel-only response. In the revised manuscript, we focused on
the paclitaxel plus cisplatin regimens of NACT throughout our investigation, which
now accurately reflects the paclitaxel and cisplatin NACT response. Additionally, in the
previous manuscript, we acknowledged that overall survival was not an appropriate
metric. Instead, we analyzed transcript expression associated with pathologic response
prior to surgery, as shown in Figure 1g, 1j, and Supplementary Figure 7d. Upregulation
of YTHDF3, INCENP, and CDCA8 contributes to poor NACT response in ESCC.
b. In Figure 1O- time to death should be displayed as opposed to death alone-also the
authors do not mention if the patients received additional treatment after surgery and
how such treatment is weighing into their correlations.
Response: Thank you for your thoughtful comments and valuable suggestions. We
have conducted additional survival analyses of INCENP and CDCA8 expression,
incorporating time to death in Supplementary Fig. 1k. Our analysis demonstrates that
high expression levels of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 in non-responders are
associated with shorter survival times (line 144).
We agree that patients often receive additional adjuvant treatments after surgery, and
that the 5-year survival rate is influenced by multiple factors, while there is no clear
consensus in the literature regarding which specific adjuvant therapies significantly
improve the 5-year survival rate after NACT. However, it is well established that
achieving pathological complete response (pCR) after NACT is a strong and reliable
prognostic indicator. Numerous studies have reported that pCR is associated with
significantly improved 5-year survival rates and better overall prognosis. In line with
this, our clinical information analysis data also demonstrated that responders exhibit
significantly longer overall survival (OS) and progression-free survival (PFS)
(Supplementary Fig. 7b, c). Therefore, the biomarkers we identified for predicting the
potential for pCR after NACT, and their relationship to patient prognosis. These
biomarkers may provide valuable insights into which patients are most likely to benefit
from NACT, helping to personalize treatment strategies and ultimately improve patient
outcomes. We clarified this concern in manuscript discussion (line 350).
Reference:
--Meredith KL, Weber JM, Turaga KK, et al. Pathologic response after neoadjuvant
therapy is the major determinant of survival in patients with esophageal cancer. Ann
Surg Oncol 2010;17:1159–1167.
--E Ancona, A Ruol, S Santi, et al. Only pathologic complete response to neoadjuvant
chemotherapy improves significantly the long term survival of patients with resectable
esophageal squamous cell carcinoma: final report of a randomized, controlled trial of
preoperative chemotherapy versus surgery alone. Cancer 2001;91:2165–2174.
--Farrukh Hassan Rizvi, Aamir Ali Syed, Shahid Khattak, et al. Complete pathological

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
While authors revised the manuscript substantially, there are still several concerns.
1, The upregulation of YTHDF3 in cancer and its regulation of gene expression in an m6A-
dependent manner are not novel at all. As both INCENP and CDCA8 are critical regulator of
cell division, KD or OE is not surprising to affect the chemosensitivity. Therefore, the
mechanistic insights are quite limited to achieve a conceptual advance for the field.
Response: We thank the reviewer for taking the time to assess our manuscript. We
respectfully need to highlight the following key points regarding the novelty and
significance of our study:
1. Unique Contribution of INCENP and CDCA8 in Clinical Significance:
Resistance to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) poses a major clinical challenge,
and reliable biomarkers to guide patient selection are urgently needed. Here, our study
identifies INCENP and CDCA8 as previously unrecognized modulators of
chemotherapy sensitivity in ESCC. Functional experiments, followed by in-depth
mechanistic investigations, reveal their critical roles in mediating the cellular response
to chemotherapy, thereby establishing a direct functional link between these genes and
chemotherapy sensitivity. Importantly, this association is further validated in
independent cohorts from lung and breast cancers, underscoring the potential of
INCENP and CDCA8 as predictive biomarkers for chemotherapy response beyond
ESCC.
2, Novel mechanism
This study uncovers a novel mechanism that INCENP and CDCA8 transcripts
undergo m6A modification, a key epigenetic regulation, and are recognized by
YTHDF3, which promotes their translation by interacting with eIF3A, driving NACT
resistance. Crucially, the efficacy of these chemotherapeutic agents is dependent on the
m6A modification status of INCENP and CDCA8, marking a previously unrecognized
regulatory layer in chemotherapy response. Inhibition of INCENP and CDCA8 leads to
the formation of multipolar spindle, sensitizing cells to NACT in both in vitro and in
vivo models. These findings highlight how m⁶A epigenetic modification of INCENP
and CDCA8 transcripts leads to mitotic dysregulation, which collectively contributes to
NACT response.
3. Novel Role of YTHDF3 in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma:
We need to emphasis that the role of YTHDF3 in ESCC has not been previously
characterized. Our work is the first to reveal its upregulation and mitosis-regulated
function in ESCC, especially in the context of chemotherapy response.
Taken together, these findings reveal novel mechanisms driving NACT resistance
and identify reliable predictive biomarkers, highlighting the clinical relevance of
INCENP and CDCA8 in guiding personalized NACT strategies. This is particularly
valuable given the current lack of reliable predictors for chemosensitivity in cancer
patients. The integration of mitotic gene expression into clinical decision-making
represents a step forward in precision oncology.
2, Authors emphasizes on the clinical relevance which support their submission to this
journal. However, this part are much weak even non-sense at all. Analysis based on post-
surgical samples are completely misleading. How can it PREDICT the response of NACT which
are given before the operation? Pre-treatment biopsy tissues, rather than post-surgical
samples, should be used.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. We fully agree that pre-
treatment biopsy samples are critical for assessing predictive biomarkers of NAC
response. To address this, we have analyzed the expression levels of INCENP and
CDCA8 in pre-treatment biopsy tissues from ESCC, lung and breast cancer patients
undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy, the results revealed significantly higher
expression levels of INCENP, CDCA8 and YTHDF3 in non-responders compared to
responders across all three cancer types. Notably, in ESCC, non-responders with high
expression of these genes exhibited markedly shorter progression-free survival (PFS).
Furthermore, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses demonstrated that
YTHDF3, INCENP and CDCA8 possess significant predictive potential for NACT
response in ESCC, breast, and lung cancers. These findings support the clinical utility
of INCENP and CDCA8 as predictive biomarkers across cancer types. We have revised
the manuscript (line 341) and the corresponding results in Figure. 7 and supplementary
figure. 7.
3, How dare to use “pa-cancer” in the title while most studies are using ESCC cell lines and
ESCC tissues?
Response: We thank the reviewer’s thoughtful feedback. Our study indeed investigates
the roles of INCENP and CDCA8 as predictive factors for neoadjuvant chemotherapy
sensitivity, not only in ESCC but also in lung and breast cancer. Hence, the term "pan-
cancer" was used to reflect the broader scope of our findings across different cancer
types. However, we accept your suggestion and revise the title to "INCENP and CDCA8
predict neoadjuvant chemotherapy response and outcomes in esophageal squamous
cell carcinoma" as you recommended.
4, What is m6A methylation of INCENP (at alanine 113) and CDCA8 (at alanine 1041)
transcripts？
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s detailed and helpful suggestions. Our previous
description may have caused misunderstanding. To clarify, we revised to convey that

1041) of CDCA8 undergo m⁶A methylation and are recognized by YTHDF3”. (line30)

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT), a key strategy for various cancers, markedly improves patient prognosis and 5-year survival rates. However, numerous patients develop resistance to NACT and thus fail to benefit from it. Therefore, identifying reliable biomarkers to predict patient responsiveness to NACT remains a critical challenge. Here, we demonstrate that elevated expression of INCENP and CDCA8 contributes to poor NACT responsiveness across multiple cancers. Mechanistically, the 5′ UTR (GGACT at position 113) of INCENP and the 3′ UTR (GGACT at position 1041) of CDCA8 undergo m⁶A methylation and are recognized by YTHDF3, which facilitates their translation through interaction with eIF3A, ultimately driving poor response to NACT. Moreover, inhibition of INCENP and CDCA8 enhances NACT sensitivity by promoting multipolar spindle formation. Collectively, our findings establish that INCENP and CDCA8 serve as crucial biomarkers for predicting NACT responsiveness and as potential therapeutic targets for combination therapy with NACT to improve patient survival.

---

## Introduction

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) has become a standard treatment for patients with various cancers undergoing surgery, particularly in lung cancer, breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and esophageal cancer1–4. It aims to reduce tumor size, improve surgical resectability, and lower the risk of postoperative recurrence. Among the commonly used NACT regimens, paclitaxel plus cisplatin is a primary first-line treatment for several malignancies5–7. Although this regimen is considered highly cytotoxic to tumors, its response rate in esophageal cancer remains limited at approximately 50–60%8,9. Notably, a subset of patients exhibits resistance to NACT, leading to tumor progression and significantly compromising both survival outcomes and quality of life10,11. Therefore, identifying reliable predictive biomarkers for NACT sensitivity is essential for guiding personalized treatment.

The mechanisms underlying resistance to NACT are complex, including tumor microenvironment influences and molecular heterogeneity of cancers12,13. Among these, dysregulation of the cell cycle has emerged as a key contributor. Mitosis is a fundamental biological process that regulates cell division and serves as a crucial therapeutic target in overcoming paclitaxel resistance14,15. Overexpression of mitotic regulators, such as cyclins and checkpoint proteins, can effectively halt or repair damage in mitosis, thereby diminishing the efficacy of paclitaxel16,17. Conversely, targeting these regulators, which leads to chromosomal instability or maintains multipolar spindles throughout mitosis, can improve the clinical utility of paclitaxel18,19. Additionally, cisplatin resistance has been linked to dysregulation of cell cycle-associated proteins20,21. In this study, we focus on the chromosomal passenger complex (CPC), a key mitotic regulator composed of Aurora B kinase, inner centromere protein (INCENP), survivin, and cell division cycle-associated 8 (CDCA8). The CPC plays a central role in mitosis by orchestrating chromatin-induced microtubule stabilization, chromosome bi-orientation, and spindle assembly checkpoint regulation22–24. However, the role of CPC in regulating NACT resistance remains unexplored.

Emerging evidence suggests that epigenetic modifications, particularly abnormal N6-methyladenosine (m6A) methylation, contribute to malignancy progression25. m6A modifications regulate gene expression through RNA methyltransferases (writers), demethylases (erasers), and m6A-binding proteins (readers), all of which are frequently dysregulated in various tumor types26,27. Recent studies indicate that m6A modification plays a key role in drug resistance via multiple molecular pathways28,29; however, the role of m6A in mitotic regulation and its impact on NACT response remain poorly understood. Therefore, further investigation is required to elucidate the role of m6A methylation in NACT resistance.

In this study, we identify INCENP and CDCA8 as key predictors of poor response to NACT across multiple cancer types. We demonstrate that m6A methylation of INCENP and CDCA8 mRNAs is catalyzed by METTL3 and recognized by YTHDF3, which promotes their translation by interacting with eIF3A, thereby contributing to NACT resistance. Importantly, the efficacy of these chemotherapeutic agents is dependent on the m6A modification status of INCENP and CDCA8. Inhibition of INCENP and CDCA8 leads to the formation of a multipolar spindle, thereby enhancing sensitivity to NACT both in vitro and in vivo. These results provide a strong rationale for exploring combination therapies that target INCENP and CDCA8 to improve NACT responsiveness across multiple cancers.

---

## Results

Upregulation of INCENP and CDCA8 contributes to poor NACT response
To identify potential drivers of NACT response, we performed transcriptomic profiling of clinical esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) tissue samples from NACT recipients (Cohort 1, Supplementary Data 1) following the study design (Fig. 1a). Patients with evaluable responses were classified as responders (TRG0, 1) and non-responders (TRG2, 3) based on the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) TRG criteria30. To explore the mechanisms regulating NACT response, we began with gene ontology (GO) analysis, which revealed that differentially expressed genes (DEGs) converge on key regulators of cell division (Fig. 1b). Consistent with these findings, Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analysis revealed significant alterations in cell cycle pathways (Supplementary Fig. 1a), highlighting the crucial role of cell mitotic regulation in NACT response. Additionally, we observed that the N6-methyladenosine-containing RNA binding function ranked as the top-enriched molecular function (Fig. 1b), and m6A modification plays a critical role in RNA metabolism by regulating gene expression through modulation of mRNA stability, translation efficiency, and splicing31. More importantly, emerging evidence suggests that dynamic m6A modifications play a significant role in chemotherapy resistance32,33. Therefore, we hypothesize that m6A modification modulates the progression of the mitotic pathway by regulating the RNA metabolism of mitosis-related genes, thereby driving a poor response to NACT. To address this, we analyzed the differential expression of 20 m6A regulators in Cohort 1 (Fig. 1c) and found a markedly elevated YTHDF3 expression in non-responder samples (Supplementary Fig. 1b). These findings suggest that YTHDF3 upregulation plays a significant role in the poor response to NACT in ESCC.

We further investigated whether YTHDF3, as an upstream m6A regulator, modulates the mitotic pathway and identified candidate mitosis-related genes that may contribute to poor NACT responsiveness. Therefore, we employed a functional proteomics analysis using YTHDF3 knockdown (KD) ESCC cells. Initially, we analyzed the variation in KEGG pathways, and surprisingly, the results indicated enrichment of numerous proteins involved in the cell cycle (Supplementary Fig. 1c). More importantly, GO enrichment analysis highlighted the chromosomal passenger complex in the cellular component section as the top altered pathway in shYTHDF3 ESCC cells (Fig. 1d). Moreover, Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) revealed a negative association between genes involved in mitotic nuclear division (Fig. 1e, Supplementary Fig. 1d) in YTHDF3 KD cells. Additionally, the core components of the CPC, including INCENP, CDCA8, and AURKB, were significantly downregulated in shYTHDF3 cells. Notably, expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 showed more pronounced changes in both shYTHDF3 and YTHDF3 over-expressing (OE) ESCC cell lines (Supplementary Fig. 1e–h); therefore, we focused on INCENP and CDCA8 as potential targets for further investigation. We subsequently verified that the expression of INCENP, CDCA8 and YTHDF3 proteins was upregulated in non-responders of cohort 1 clinical samples by immunohistochemical staining (IHC) (Fig. 1f, g), and that the expression of INCENP and CDCA8 was positively correlated with YTHDF3 levels (Fig. 1h). Collectively, by integrating transcriptomic profiling of Cohort 1, proteomics analysis of shYTHDF3 cells, and pathological examination of protein expression, we demonstrate that INCENP and CDCA8, as cell mitotic regulators modulated by YTHDF3, may contribute to poor NACT response in ESCC patients.

To further confirm that elevated expression of INCENP and CDCA8 is associated with poor response to NACT in ESCC patients, we analyzed another clinical cohort (Cohort 2, Supplementary Data 2). Radiological images indicated that tumor size was significantly reduced in responders, and IHC results revealed markedly higher INCENP and CDCA8 expression in tissue samples from non-responders (Fig. 1i, j) and in cancer tissues from ESCC tissue arrays (Supplementary Fig. 1i, j, Supplementary Data 3). These findings suggest that the upregulation of INCENP and CDCA8 contributes to poor response to NACT and is associated with ESCC progression. Furthermore, elevated expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 were associated with poor clinical outcomes, including disease progression (Fig. 1k) and shorter survival times in ESCC patients receiving NACT (Supplementary Fig. 1k). Collectively, INCENP and CDCA8 may serve as potential drivers of NACT non-responsiveness in ESCC.

Knockdown of INCENP and CDCA8 potentiates the sensitivity of ESCC to NACT
Given the elevated expression of INCENP and CDCA8 in non-responders, we explored the impact of these proteins on the chemosensitivity of ESCC cells to paclitaxel and cisplatin. To investigate the correlation between basal expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 and the sensitivity of ESCC cell lines to paclitaxel and cisplatin, we treated a panel of ESCC cell lines with these drugs. These findings indicate that elevated basal expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 are associated with increased IC50 values, suggesting a negative correlation between their expression and the sensitivity to paclitaxel and cisplatin across ESCC cell lines. (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 2a).

To further validate the sensitizing effect of INCENP and CDCA8 KD on paclitaxel and cisplatin responses in ESCC cells, an MTT assay was utilized, and the results showed that INCENP and CDCA8 KD decreased the IC50 values of paclitaxel and cisplatin compared with mock controls (Fig. 2c, d and Supplementary Fig. 2b, c). Consistently, plate colony formation assays demonstrated that INCENP and CDCA8 KD increased the sensitivity of ESCC cells to paclitaxel and cisplatin compared with the mock control (Fig. 2e, f and Supplementary Fig. 2d, e). Furthermore, overexpression (OE) of INCENP and CDCA8 increased the IC50 values of paclitaxel and cisplatin in KYSE450 ESCC cells compared with the vector control (Fig. 2g and Supplementary Fig. 2f), with similar results observed in the plate colony formation assay (Fig. 2h). To further validate these findings, in vivo assays were conducted to examine the impact of targeting INCENP and CDCA8 on the therapeutic efficacy of paclitaxel and cisplatin. Consistent with our in vitro findings, treatment of shINCENP and shCDCA8 ESCC cells with paclitaxel or cisplatin resulted in a reduced ESCC tumor burden compared with paclitaxel- or cisplatin-treated control cells. (Fig. 2i–k). These findings support the idea that targeting INCENP and CDCA8 enhances response to NACT in ESCC.

YTHDF3 drives mitosis and NACT resistance via INCENP and CDCA8
To further investigate whether YTHDF3 acts as an upstream regulator that modulates the cell mitotic pathway and suppresses NACT responsiveness through the regulation of INCENP and CDCA8 expression, we examined cell cycle and mitotic alterations in shYTHDF3 ESCC cells. The results showed that YTHDF3 KD led to G2/M phase arrest (Fig. 3a) and decreased protein expression of G2 phase regulators (Supplementary Fig. 3a, b). Consistently, immunofluorescence (IF) results demonstrated that YTHDF3 KD induced a defective cell mitosis phenotype characterized by multipolar spindle formation in ESCC cells (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Fig. 3c, d).

To further investigate the function of YTHDF3, we used Ebselen as a selective inhibitor. Its target specificity was systematically validated by assessing the viability of YTHDF3 KD cells following Ebselen treatment (Supplementary Fig. 3e, f). Consistently, Ebselen treatment also induced G2/M phase arrest (Supplementary Fig. 3g–i) and promoted the formation of multipolar spindles in ESCC cells (Supplementary Fig. 3j, k). These findings further confirm that YTHDF3 plays a crucial role in regulating mitosis in ESCC cells.

Given the elevated expression of YTHDF3 in non-responders, we investigated its role in modulating chemosensitivity in ESCC cells. Treatment of a panel of ESCC cell lines with paclitaxel and cisplatin revealed that higher basal expression of YTHDF3 was associated with increased IC50 values, indicating reduced drug sensitivity (Supplementary Fig. 3l, m). Furthermore, YTHDF3 KD and Ebselen treatment enhanced the sensitivity of ESCC cells to paclitaxel and cisplatin compared with the control (Fig. 3c–f and Supplementary Fig. 3n, o). In contrast, YTHDF3 OE decreased the sensitivity of ESCC cells to paclitaxel and cisplatin compared with the vector control (Fig. 3g, h and Supplementary Fig. 3p). In vivo studies revealed that Ebselen sensitized ESCC cells to paclitaxel (Fig. 3i–k) and cisplatin treatment (Fig. 3l–n), as evidenced by reduced tumor size and weight. Importantly, no significant differences in total body weight were associated with any treatment regimens (Supplementary Fig. 3q, r). These findings support the idea that inhibiting YTHDF3 potentiates NACT responsiveness both in vitro and in vivo.

To determine whether the effect of YTHDF3 on NACT response is functionally dependent on INCENP and CDCA8, we examined the impact of their overexpression in YTHDF3 KD cells. We found that INCENP and CDCA8 OE reversed the enhanced sensitivity to paclitaxel and cisplatin caused by YTHDF3 KD, resulting in decreased drug sensitivity (Fig. 3o, p and Supplementary Fig. 3s, t). These findings support the notion that both INCENP and CDCA8 are essential for proper mitotic progression and functionally act as downstream effectors of YTHDF3. Collectively, our results suggest that the effect of YTHDF3 on NACT responsiveness depends on INCENP and CDCA8.

INCENP and CDCA8 mRNAs are m6A-methylated and recognized by YTHDF3 to modulate NACT response
To elucidate whether YTHDF3 regulates INCENP and CDCA8 expression in an m6A-dependent manner, we assessed the requirement of its m6A-binding ability in this regulatory process. YTHDF3 contains two hydrophobic residues W438 and W492, which are integral to the specific recognition of m6A31,34. To examine this, we constructed a YTHDF3 mutant (YTHDF3-mut) plasmid (Supplementary Fig. 4a) and transfected both WT and YTHDF3-mut plasmids into YTHDF3 KD cells. As expected, the decreased expression of CDCA8 and INCENP in YTHDF3 KD cells was rescued by ectopic expression of WT YTHDF3, but not by the YTHDF3-mut (Fig. 4a, b and Supplementary Fig. 4b, c). Furthermore, G2/M phase arrest (Fig. 4c) and reduced expression of G2 phase regulator (Fig. 4d and Supplementary Fig. 4d) observed in YTHDF3 KD cells were reversed upon WT YTHDF3 transfection. Moreover, the formation of multipolar spindles in mitotic YTHDF3 KD ESCC cells was rescued by WT YTHDF3 overexpression, but not by the mutant YTHDF3 (Fig. 4e, f). Collectively, these findings suggest that YTHDF3 regulates the expression of INCENP and CDCA8 in an m6A-dependent manner and plays a pivotal role in cell mitosis.

To further investigate how CDCA8 and INCENP transcripts undergo m6A modification, we analyzed the GEPIA database and observed a positive correlation between the expression of the RNA methyltransferase METTL3 and the levels of both INCENP and CDCA8 (Supplementary Fig. 4e), and METTL3 expression was examined to identify its role in the m6A modification of these transcripts. Subsequently, we generated stable cell lines with low levels of m6A decoration by METTL3 KD (Supplementary Fig. 4f). We observed reduced protein levels of CDCA8 and INCENP in both METTL3 KD cells (Fig. 4g and Supplementary Fig. 4g, h) and ESCC patient-derived xenograft organoids (PDXO) (Fig. 4h–k and Supplementary Fig. 4i). Moreover, multipolar spindle formation was observed in mitotic METTL3 KD cells (Fig. 4l, m and Supplementary Fig. 4j). These data collectively demonstrate that YTHDF3 regulates METTL3-mediated N⁶-methylation of CDCA8 and INCENP transcripts in an m⁶A-dependent manner. More importantly, METTL3 expression was significantly higher in non-responder tissues compared to responder tissues (Fig. 4n, o). Further analysis revealed that METTL3 expression was positively correlated with INCENP and CDCA8 expression (Fig. 4p), thereby identifying N6-methylation of INCENP and CDCA8 transcripts as a key factor associated with poor NACT responsiveness in ESCC cells.

YTHDF3 promotes the translation of INCENP and CDCA8 mRNAs
Given that the expression of INCENP and CDCA8 proteins was decreased in shYTHDF3 ESCC cells (Supplementary Fig. 1e, f) and PDXO (Fig. 5a, b and Supplementary Fig. 5a, b), we sought to elucidate the molecular mechanisms by which YTHDF3 regulates INCENP and CDCA8. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-seq) analysis revealed direct binding of YTHDF3 protein to both INCENP and CDCA8 transcripts (Fig. 5c, d), which was subsequently confirmed by RIP-qPCR assays (Fig. 5e). Given that YTHDF3 facilitates translation and decay of N6-methyladenosine-modified RNA31, we next examined whether YTHDF3 knockdown affected target mRNA abundance. qRT-PCR results showed that the mRNA levels of INCENP and CDCA8 were unaffected by YTHDF3 KD (Supplementary Fig. 5c), suggesting that the observed protein downregulation likely occurs at the translational level. Indeed, the nascently synthesized proteins on ESCC cell lines overexpressing Flag-YTHDF3 were increased compared to the vector control group as determined by a protein synthesis assay (Fig. 5f, g) and the Surface Sensing of Translation (SUnSET) assay (Supplementary Fig. 5d). To further investigate, we constructed pmirGLO-CDCA8 and pmirGLO-INCENP luciferase reporters. The dual-luciferase assay showed that the translation efficiency of CDCA8 and INCENP was significantly lower in YTHDF3 KD ESCC cells compared with mock cells (Fig. 5h, i). Collectively, these findings indicate that YTHDF3 regulates the translation of CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs.

To elucidate the underlying mechanism by which YTHDF3 regulates the translation of INCENP and CDCA8, we performed co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) to identify proteins associated with translation regulation, including eEF1A2, RPS3A, eIF4A1, and eIF3A (Supplementary Fig. 5e). Our results demonstrated that YTHDF3 interacts with eIF3A, a component of the eukaryotic translation initiation factor (eIF) complex, as confirmed by both co-IP and IF assays (Fig. 5j, k and Supplementary Fig. 5f, g). To further confirm the direct interaction between YTHDF3 and eIF3A, we performed a proximity ligation assay (PLA), which illustrated the distribution of in situ PLA spots of YTHDF3-eIF3A in the cell cytoplasm (Fig. 5l, m). To investigate whether YTHDF3 regulates the translation of INCENP and CDCA8 through eIF3A, we performed eIF3A RIP-qPCR and found that both YTHDF3 KD and Ebselen treatments significantly reduced the binding of eIF3A to CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs (Fig. 5n, o and Supplementary Fig. 5h). Additionally, ESCC cells treated with Ebselen showed reduced binding of YTHDF3 to CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 5i), leading to decreased protein expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 (Supplementary Fig. 5j, k). Collectively, these findings highlight that YTHDF3 enhances the translation of CDCA8 and INCENP by recruiting eIF3A to its target mRNAs.

To further investigate whether YTHDF3 regulates CDCA8 and INCENP translation in an m6A-dependent manner. RIP-qPCR was performed, and the results showed that YTHDF3 and eIF3A bind more strongly to CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs in ESCC cells overexpressing WT YTHDF3, but not in cells expressing mutant YTHDF3 (Supplementary Fig. 5l, m). Additionally, dual luciferase assays demonstrated a significant increase in the translation efficiency of CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs in YTHDF3 KD ESCC cells ectopically expressing WT YTHDF3, compared with those expressing mutant YTHDF3 (Supplementary Fig. 5n). Moreover, RIP-qPCR assays showed that the binding of YTHDF3 and eIF3A to m6A-modified CDCA8 and INCENP mRNAs was significantly reduced in METTL3 KD cells (Fig. 5p, q). These findings collectively suggest that YTHDF3 regulates the translation of CDCA8 and INCENP in an m6A-dependent manner.

INCENP and CDCA8 contribute to poor NACT response in an m6A-dependent manner
Based on our findings that m6A modification of INCENP and CDCA8 mRNAs is indispensable for YTHDF3 recognition and regulation, it is essential to explore the m6A modification sites of INCENP and CDCA8 mRNAs for the regulation of NACT response in ESCC cells. Very high-confidence m6A modification sites were predicted using the SRAMP web tool (www.cuilab.cn/sramp) (Fig. 6a, b). Methylated RNA immunoprecipitation followed by qPCR (meRIP-qPCR) results showed that, among the predicted m⁶A regions of INCENP, the 5′ UTR m⁶A site (site 1: GGACT at position 113) exhibited the most pronounced decrease in methylation upon METTL3 KD in ESCC cells (Fig. 6c, Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). For CDCA8, the CDS region (site 2: TGACT at position 909) and the 3′ UTR region (site 4: GGACT at position 1041) showed the greatest reduction in m⁶A levels following METTL3 KD (Fig. 6d, Supplementary Fig. 6c, d). Dual-luciferase reporter assays further demonstrated that mutation of the 5′ UTR m⁶A site in INCENP, as well as mutations of the 3′ UTR and dual-site regions in CDCA8, significantly reduced translation efficiency in ESCC cells, whereas mutation of the CDS m⁶A site alone in CDCA8 had no detectable effect (Supplementary Fig. 6e, f). Collectively, these data indicate that the 5′ UTR (GGACT at position 113) of INCENP and the 3′ UTR (GGACT at position 1041) of CDCA8 undergo METTL3-mediated m⁶A modification, which contributes to their translation regulation in ESCC.

To elucidate whether CDCA8 and INCENP contribute to the poor response to NACT through these m6A modification sites, we overexpressed either WT or double-mutant CDCA8 (mut-CDCA8) and 5’UTR-mutant INCENP (mut-INCENP) in YTHDF3 KD ESCC cell lines. We found that the frequency of multipolar spindle formation observed in YTHDF3 KD ESCC cells was decreased upon expression of WT INCENP or CDCA8 (Fig. 6e, f). To determine whether m6A modification of INCENP and CDCA8 plays a pivotal role in NACT responsiveness, we assessed the sensitivity of YTHDF3 KD ESCC cells to paclitaxel and cisplatin following transfection with either WT or m⁶A site–mutant INCENP and CDCA8 constructs. Our results showed that paclitaxel and cisplatin sensitivity was reduced in YTHDF3 KD cells transfected with WT INCENP or CDCA8 plasmids, but not in those transfected with the m⁶A site–mutant constructs (Fig. 6g, h and Supplementary Fig. 6g, h). These findings indicate that the ability of INCENP and CDCA8 to modulate the NACT response is dependent on their m⁶A methylation. Collectively, INCENP and CDCA8 transcripts are N6-methylated by METTL3 and subsequently recognized by YTHDF3, which promotes their translation via interaction with eIF3A, ultimately leading to paclitaxel and cisplatin resistance in ESCC (Fig. 6i).

INCENP and CDCA8 serve as predictors of poor NACT response across multiple cancer types
Given the contribution of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 to poor NACT response, we retrospectively analyzed their expression levels in relation to clinical outcomes using a cohort of 65 pre-treatment biopsy samples from ESCC patients (Cohort 3, Supplementary Data 4). Based on annotated clinical and molecular attributes of individual patient data, we observed that non-responders were more likely to present with advanced TNM stages and medullary histological types (Fig. 7a and Supplementary Fig. 7a), suggesting a correlation between these clinical parameters and NACT response. IHC staining revealed that responders exhibited significantly lower expression levels of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 compared with non-responders in biopsy tissues from ESCC (Fig. 7b, c). Given the widespread use of the paclitaxel plus cisplatin regimen as an NACT strategy across multiple cancer types35–37. We extended our analysis to assess the protein expression levels of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 in response to this regimen in breast and lung cancer patients from Cohort 3. IHC results revealed that patients who responded favorably to NACT exhibited significantly lower expression levels of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 compared with non-responders (Fig. 7b, d, e). Furthermore, expression levels of INCENP and CDCA8 showed a positive correlation with YTHDF3 expression (Fig. 7f and Supplementary Fig. 7b, c). Collectively, these findings demonstrate that INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 are upregulated in multiple cancer types, supporting the pivotal role of the YTHDF3-m6A-CDCA8/INCENP axis in driving poor NACT responsiveness across multiple cancers.

To further investigate the prognostic relevance of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 expression in the context of NACT, we performed survival analysis. Results revealed that responders exhibited significantly longer progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) compared with non-responders (Supplementary Fig. 7d, e). Notably, among non-responders, high expression of INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3 proteins was associated with significantly shorter PFS in ESCC patients (Fig. 7g–i), suggesting that elevated levels of these proteins are correlated with poor clinical outcomes following NACT. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves were generated for each biomarker across multiple cancer types to evaluate their predictive performance, reflecting the sensitivity and specificity of these predictors. The results revealed area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.785, 0.736, and 0.707 for INCENP, CDCA8, and YTHDF3, respectively. Importantly, a combined analysis of these biomarkers demonstrated superior predictive accuracy, with an AUC of 0.817 in ESCC (Fig. 7j). These findings indicate that a composite biomarker model provides more accurate prediction of poor NACT response in ESCC patients. Additionally, in both lung and breast cancers, YTHDF3, INCENP, and CDCA8 also exhibited significant potential as predictors of NACT response (Fig. 7k, l). Collectively, these results highlight the critical role of YTHDF3, INCENP, and CDCA8 as robust and broadly applicable predictors of NACT responsiveness across multiple cancer types, with enhanced accuracy achieved through combined assessment.
